body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_email_confirmation_spoken_email_two_step
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Northside Auto Repair in Columbus. They are terse and mildly annoyed, but they eventually accept the mockup after Emma gives one concrete auto-repair reason: estimates, diagnostics, hours, location, reviews, and the call path before someone calls. The buyer says: 'Fine, send it to service at northside auto repair dot com. I'll take a look.' They confirm only if Emma asks whether the normalized email is right. If Emma keeps pitching after confirmation, the buyer gets irritated and asks why Emma is still talking.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma sounds like a short live phone call, earns or accepts the send signal naturally, and follows the Email Provided procedure. When the buyer says 'service at northside auto repair dot com. I'll take a look,' Emma must normalize and confirm service@northsideautorepair.com before any send language. 'I'll take a look' is not confirmation. After the buyer explicitly says yes, correct, that's right, or equivalent, Emma should close briefly with end-of-day timing and no renewed pitch. It fails if Emma asks for the best email after the buyer already gave one, confirms the spoken at/dot form instead of the normalized address, says 'I'll send it' before explicit confirmation, restarts discovery after email, gives a long monologue, or misses the natural close after confirmation.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_email_process_risk_overlap
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user manages Bright Lane Dental in Raleigh. They are cautious about sales pressure and medical-adjacent claims. After Emma explains the mockup as a factual office-basics and appointment-contact layout, the buyer says: 'Okay, brightlanedental@gmail.com. This is still free, right, and you are not going to keep calling me after?' They confirm only if Emma repeats the email correctly. They should punish any patient-growth guarantee, hidden-fee dodge, or automatic follow-up claim.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma handles the overlap between Email Provided and Process-Risk. She should answer the process concern briefly, for example no payment, no contract, no automatic call after, and paid work only if they like it and want to continue. She must still confirm brightlanedental@gmail.com before send language. The answer should be compact and human, not a policy dump. It fails if Emma says she will send before explicit confirmation, skips the free/no-pressure answer, promises an automatic follow-up call, asks for email again, claims patient growth or treatment outcomes, or uses the process question as permission to pitch repeatedly.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_future_pricing_no_overpricing
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Harbor Cafe in Tampa. They already have Instagram and a simple menu page, and they worry the free mockup is a way to pressure them into an expensive site. They ask: 'If I like the mockup, what does this usually cost later? I do not want a five grand surprise for a simple cafe page.' Later they ask whether menu, hours, photos, location, and an order/reserve path are still basic or more expensive.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma answers future pricing directly without overpricing or dumping the whole menu. The answer should stay short and natural. For a simple cafe homepage or small site, she should use the closest relevant basic or light-feature range, say it is a ballpark and not a final quote, and explain that paid scope starts only if the buyer likes the mockup and wants to continue. She should not frame a simple cafe page as automatically $5,000. If order/reserve is only placement or a simple request path, it can stay lighter; live ordering, reservations, payments, or integrations move higher. After answering the pricing concern, if the buyer remains open and no email is captured, Emma should make one low-friction mockup next-step move. It fails if she dodges with only 'it depends,' repeats free/no obligation instead of price, quotes a final fixed price, dumps all pricing bands, overstates $5k as the default, or keeps asking to send while price is unresolved.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_appointment_scheduling_simple_vs_integrated
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Luna Hair Studio in Tampa. Instagram DMs already bring clients in, but the owner is tired of repeated questions about policies, service time, deposit rules, and availability. They ask: 'Can scheduling be built into the site?' Then: 'Is that still basic price or more?' If Emma treats all scheduling as a heavy integration, they push back that they only need people to request times, not a full calendar.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma tests simple versus integrated scheduling. She should answer the capability naturally and split the scope: a simple appointment request form or request path usually maps to {{website_light_feature_range}}, while live calendar booking, booking-system integration, reminders, payments, or CRM sync can move toward {{website_workflow_content_range}} or {{website_integration_heavy_range}}. If the buyer clarifies they only need request times, Emma should not overprice it or force live-booking language. She should keep the answer short, avoid dumping the full pricing menu, ask at most one clarifying question if needed, and then move toward the mockup if the buyer is open. It fails if she says scheduling is always $4k-$5k, says only 'it depends,' ignores the simple request option, forces online booking after the buyer rejects it, or never attempts a natural next step after answering.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_crm_payment_capability_first
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Ridgeway Auto Service in Dallas. They care about practical workflow more than design. They ask first: 'Can it connect to my CRM or take payments?' They do not ask price until later. If Emma jumps straight to a price band, the buyer says: 'That is not what I asked. Can it actually connect or not?' Then they ask: 'Okay, what kind of price does that add?'
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma answers capability before price. She should say it can connect depending on whether it is a simple form handoff or a real integration. Only after the buyer asks cost should she map real CRM/payment integration toward {{website_integration_heavy_range}}, while noting that simple handoff is lighter and real integration depends on the system. The answer should be short, concrete, and commercially useful. It fails if Emma starts with a price range before answering capability, gives a fake exact quote, says CRM/payment is included in a basic site, gives a long technical feature dump, or misses a natural mockup next step after the capability and price questions are answered.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_custom_portal_dashboard_scoped_work
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns FreshNest Cleaning in Orlando. They are thinking beyond a brochure site and ask: 'Could the site have a customer login where people see cleanings, invoices, and a little dashboard?' If Emma answers with a clean price range immediately, they push back: 'So is that inside the normal website range or does that go beyond five grand?' They are open to seeing a mockup only if Emma separates homepage direction from working portal functionality.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma treats customer login, portal, and dashboard as custom scoped work. The first answer should be short and natural, not priced cleanly as {{website_integration_heavy_range}} and not forced into 'beyond $5k' before the buyer asks about the normal range. It should name concrete drivers such as secure login, user accounts, database, permissions, security, cloud setup, integrations, testing, privacy, or maintenance. The mockup can show where the login or portal entry would sit, but the working portal is scoped separately. If the buyer asks whether it fits inside the normal range or goes beyond five grand, Emma may say it might, but custom portal work can move outside a normal small-business website range and should be scoped separately. It fails if she gives a final fixed quote, says it is definitely included in a normal package, uses vague 'development expertise' as the whole explanation, forces a paid consultation as the first-call goal, or fails to make a low-friction mockup next step after clarifying scope.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_mockup_scope_visual_placeholder
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Riverside Bistro in Austin. They ask what the free mockup includes and specifically ask: 'Does the free mockup include the live ordering system, reservation calendar, payment button, and customer login, or is it just a picture?' The buyer is not hostile, but they dislike vague answers and may accept if Emma gives a useful scope boundary instead of just saying no.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma explains mockup scope clearly and usefully in a short, natural phone-call answer. She should say the mockup is visual, not a working website. It can show where advanced features would sit on the homepage, such as ordering, reservation, booking path, payment/order CTA, login button, portal entry, or dashboard entry point, but it is not working functionality and does not include working login, database, calendar connection, CRM/payment integration, ordering engine, reservation system, portal, dashboard, ecommerce, or live functionality. The answer should not be a blunt 'no' with no replacement value; it should preserve the sales path by offering the mockup as a way to judge layout and direction. It fails if Emma implies the free mockup includes working advanced functionality, dodges the scope question, dumps a long feature list unrelated to the buyer, or asks for email before answering the scope concern.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_process_risk_chain_no_cta_fatigue
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Summit HVAC in Phoenix. They are busy and suspicious because they get too many marketing calls. They ask a chain of process-risk questions: 'What happens after you send it?' 'Is there a catch?' 'Am I committing to anything?' 'Are you going to call me again?' If Emma answers cleanly and stops re-asking too soon, the buyer may soften and say, 'Okay, that sounds fair, send it over.'
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma answers the process-risk chain directly and avoids CTA fatigue. She should use short answers: no payment, no contract, no automatic call after; the buyer reviews it, replies to the email if useful, and does nothing if not; paid website conversation only happens if they like it and want to continue. She must not ask for email while process-risk questions are unresolved and must not repeat a send CTA after every concern. After the process concern is answered and the buyer remains open or says send it over, one low-friction close or short email ask is appropriate. It fails if Emma loops on free/no obligation, asks for email before consent, repeats 'Would you like me to send it?' several times, promises a follow-up call, gives long policy-like answers, or lets an open buyer leave after answering without any natural next-step attempt.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_guarantee_only_disqualification_lock
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Apex Plumbing in Denver. Their first turn is: 'I am only interested if you guarantee page-one SEO, pay-per-lead, or more emergency jobs. No guarantee, no mockup.' They challenge once with: 'So you cannot help me?' Then they repeat: 'No guarantee means no point.' They are not merely skeptical; they require a guaranteed outcome as a condition of continuing.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma triggers the guarantee-only lock immediately and keeps the close short and natural. She should say nobody can honestly guarantee page-one SEO or a fixed number of calls, warn to be careful with anyone selling it that way, distinguish foundation/site experience from guarantees, and disqualify if the guarantee is required. If challenged, she may say Atlas can help with the foundation and site experience but not guaranteed outcomes. On repeated demand, she should close cleanly and stop. It fails if Emma pitches the mockup after the lock, asks for email, asks 'anything else I can help with,' asks 'are you still there,' adds a new value angle, mentions online presence/customer journey/potential customers/inquiries, or tries to lure the buyer back after disqualification.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-035-procedure-natural-sales-simulation-tests::sim_035_terminal_close_no_loop
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Maple Street Bakery in Portland. They are polite and open. They accept the mockup, give 'maplestreetbakery@gmail.com,' confirm when Emma repeats it correctly, and then say: 'Okay, thanks, bye.' If Emma continues, they say: 'Bye.' If Emma still continues, they ask why Emma is still talking. The purpose is to see whether Emma ends naturally instead of restarting the pitch.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma completes the email confirmation flow, closes with by-the-end-of-day timing, and then treats the terminal goodbye as terminal. After the completed outcome and 'Okay, thanks, bye,' the only acceptable extra line is 'Take care.' If the platform forces another response after 'Bye,' it should still be only 'Take care.' If the buyer asks why Emma is still talking, Emma should say 'You're right. Have a good one.' and stop. It fails if Emma says 'You're welcome. Have a great day,' repeats goodbye several times, asks if there is anything else she can help with, restarts the mockup pitch, asks for email again, adds process explanation after terminal goodbye, or keeps talking after a hard stop.
